name: Denmark
summary: High-tax option. Share gains and dividends are taxed at 42% above a small band (27% up to DKK 79,400), with annual mark-to-market on many funds and an exit tax on shares. No wealth tax. Children pay 15% estate duty above an allowance of DKK 392,300 per estate; the new government proposes 30% on estates above DKK 10 million (not yet law).

regimes.name: Ordinary tax residence
regimes.description: Full tax liability on worldwide income. The researcher/expat scheme (27% + 8% labour-market tax) covers employment income only and does not help a family living off a portfolio.
regimes.eligibility: Tax resident when having a home in Denmark and staying there, or staying 6 consecutive months.

capital_gains.summary: Gains on listed shares (Danish and foreign) are 'share income' taxed on realisation at 27% on the first DKK 79,400 (2026; DKK 158,800 for a married couple) and 42% above. A large gain is therefore taxed at effectively 42%. Many funds/ETFs are instead taxed annually on unrealised gains (mark-to-market). Real-estate gains (not the main home) are capital income, taxed at up to about 42%.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: 27% band: DKK 79,400 per person (2026; 2025: DKK 67,500), doubled for spouses. Main home on a plot under 1,400 m2 is exempt (parcelhusreglen). Aktiesparekonto (share savings account): 17% annual mark-to-market on deposits up to DKK 174,200 (2026) - too small to matter for this family.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Mark-to-market (lagerprincippet): shares in investment companies (most foreign accumulating ETFs/funds) are taxed every year on unrealised value changes; those on SKAT's list of equity-based investment companies are taxed as share income (27/42%), others as capital income. Exit tax: on leaving Denmark with shares worth DKK 100,000 or more after at least 7 years of Danish tax liability, unrealised gains are taxed; deferral is available without interest (collateral required if moving outside the EU/Nordics). Foreign real estate is also subject to an exit gain rule. Announced, NOT in force (Deloitte, 3 and 24 June 2026, on the new government platform; no bill tabled as of the articles): raise the 27% share-income band to about DKK 110,000; raise the aktiesparekonto cap to DKK 500,000; a capital-taxation reform prepared by a commission; corporate tax cut from 22% to 19% over three years.

open_questions: Exact maximum marginal rate on positive net capital income (real-estate gains) under the 2026 bracket structure (new middle/top/top-top tax): PwC states 'up to 42%'; not independently recomputed.
Timing and final form of the announced capital-taxation reform and the higher 27% band (DKK ~110,000).
capital_gains.rate_basis: Top share-income rate 42% applies to a large realised gain on shares (listed or unlisted, Danish or foreign); the 27% band of DKK 79,400 is negligible for a large gain. Real estate: capital income, PwC gives a 2026 maximum of 42% (municipal + state tax on capital income, excluding church tax). No holding-period relief exists.
capital_gains.professional_trader: Share gains are share income regardless of trading frequency for individuals; there is no separate trader regime for shares. Trading in real estate can be taxed as business (personal) income at up to ~60.5% marginal (+8% labour-market contribution).
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: No holding-period exemption for shares (abolished 2006). Realisation basis for directly held shares (FIFO / average cost); mark-to-market for many investment funds.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Residents are taxed on worldwide gains. Foreign shares are not covered by Danish broker reporting; gains are self-declared. Foreign real estate gains taxed in Denmark with credit/exemption under treaties.

dividends.summary: Dividends (Danish and foreign) are share income: 27% up to DKK 79,400 (2026) and 42% above. Foreign withholding tax is credited up to the treaty rate.
dividends.exemptions_thresholds: Same 27% band as for gains (DKK 79,400 per person, shared between dividends and gains).
dividends.important_exceptions: Announced, NOT in force (Deloitte, 3 and 24 June 2026, on the new government platform; no bill tabled as of the articles): raise the 27% share-income band to about DKK 110,000; raise the aktiesparekonto cap to DKK 500,000; a capital-taxation reform prepared by a commission; corporate tax cut from 22% to 19% over three years.

dividends.rate_basis: Top share-income rate 42% for a large dividend stream; Danish dividends have 27% withheld at source, settled at final assessment. Foreign dividend tax credit is limited to the treaty rate; excess withholding must be reclaimed abroad.
dividends.withholding_outbound: 27% Danish WHT on dividends to non-residents (individuals and companies), reduced to the treaty rate via refund claims; corporate parent-subsidiary relief available.
dividends.treaty_network: Large: about 76 treaties in force per PwC (treaty with Spain terminated 2009). Note the US-Denmark treaty limits US WHT on portfolio dividends to 15%.
dividends.holding_company_notes: No holding structure is modelled for Denmark: a Danish ApS pays 22% on dividends and gains on listed portfolio shares (stakes below 10% are 'taxable portfolio shares', and listed ones are taxed annually on the mark-to-market principle), and distributions to the owners are then share income at 27%/42%, about 55% in total against 42% personally. Company-level taxation is separate (CIT 22%); distributions to the individual are share income at 27/42%. Personally owned investment companies are subject to CFC/anti-avoidance rules; check before relying on a holding structure.

wealth_tax.summary: Denmark has had no wealth tax since 1997. Owner-occupied homes pay a property value tax (ejendomsværdiskat) and municipal land tax, which are not wealth taxes.
wealth_tax.property_tax_note: Property value tax on owner-occupied homes: 0.51% of value up to DKK 9,007,000 and 1.4% above (2026, PwC). Municipal land tax (grundskyld) on land value, rate varies by municipality.
open_questions: Left-wing parties proposed a wealth tax before the 2026 election; it is not in the new government platform as summarised by Deloitte (3 June 2026). Monitor.

inheritance.summary: Estate duty (boafgift) of 15% is levied on the part of the estate passing to children after a basic allowance of DKK 392,300 per estate (2026). Lifetime gifts to children are tax-free up to DKK 80,600 per year per donor (2026); excess is taxed at 15%.
inheritance.exemptions_thresholds: Basic allowance DKK 392,300 per estate (2026), not per child. Spouses are exempt. Gift allowance DKK 80,600 per donor per child per year (2026).
inheritance.eligibility_conditions: Children, stepchildren, their descendants, parents and cohabitants of 2+ years are in the 15% class; the 25% additional duty applies only to more distant heirs.
inheritance.important_exceptions: Announced, NOT in force: the June 2026 government platform proposes raising the allowance to DKK 550,000 and adding 15 percentage points (30% total) on estates whose taxable base exceeds DKK 10 million; Deloitte understands estates with succession-qualifying (business) assets would be excluded; timing unknown, no bill tabled. Siblings move into the 15% class from 1 January 2027.
open_questions: Whether and when the proposed 30% rate on estates above DKK 10 million is enacted, and whether gift tax follows - this would materially worsen Denmark for this family.
Scope for foreign real estate of a Danish-domiciled deceased (whether excluded from the Danish estate when administered abroad) not verified.
Current rate of the reduced duty on family-business generational transfers (succession) not verified.
inheritance.gift_tax: 15% on gifts to children above DKK 80,600 per donor per year (2026); same 15% rate as estate duty.
inheritance.business_relief: Business assets can be transferred with succession (tax on latent gains deferred to the heir); gift/estate duty on business is assessed on value; portfolio holdings do not qualify (passive capital rules).
inheritance.foreign_assets: Danish estate duty applies to the estate of a person domiciled in Denmark administered in Denmark, generally worldwide assets; foreign tax credit relief.
inheritance.domicile_rules: Probate jurisdiction follows the deceased's last domicile (residence) in Denmark; no citizenship-based tail found.

residency.tax_residency_test: Full tax liability if the person has a home available in Denmark and stays there (other than short holidays), or stays in Denmark for 6 consecutive months (holidays abroad do not interrupt).

routes.name: EU/EEA free movement
routes.requirements: EU/EEA/Swiss citizens may reside with sufficient resources and register (EU residence document).

routes.name: Non-EU residence permit
routes.requirements: No investor or golden visa. Non-EU nationals need a permit (work, business, family); Denmark's immigration rules are strict. Not verified in detail.

corporate.summary: CIT 22%. Dividends paid to non-residents bear 27% WHT (refund to treaty rate). Government platform (June 2026) proposes a cut to 19% over three years; not enacted.

us_citizen_notes: US citizens remain US-taxed; the US-Denmark treaty has a saving clause. Danish mark-to-market on funds and US PFIC rules can interact badly for US persons holding non-US funds.
open_questions: Announced but unenacted reforms (estate duty 30% above DKK 10m, higher share-income band, capital-tax reform, CIT cut) should be rechecked in 2027.
